questions.text: What does parsing mean?
options: Analyzing a message, breaking it into its component parts, and understanding the purpose of each part in context
Encrypting a message before it's sent
Compressing data so it travels faster
Converting a program into machine code
questions.explanation: Background / Scenario: that's the lab's definition of parsing.

questions.text: When messages travel between computers, what are they, effectively, before they're parsed?
options: A string — a stream of characters
questions.explanation: Background / Scenario: messages travel as a stream of characters, effectively a string. It has to be parsed into an equivalent data structure of recognized types (integers, floats, strings, Booleans) before it can be acted on.

questions.text: Which data formats does the lab parse with Python? (Choose all that apply.)
questions.explanation: Objectives: Part 2 parses XML, Part 3 JSON, and Part 4 YAML.

questions.text: Why can XML be tricky to parse?
options: Its all-text tagged fields don't map unambiguously to Python's data types, and it isn't always obvious how to represent attribute values
Python has no built-in XML library
XML has to be converted to JSON before Python can read it
questions.explanation: Part 2 intro: because XML is so flexible, its all-text tagged data fields do not map unambiguously to default data types, and it is not always obvious how attribute values should be represented. (Python ships xml.etree.ElementTree, used in this lab.)

questions.text: Which Cisco tool validates and consumes XML relevant to data modeling?
questions.explanation: Part 2 intro: Cisco provides tools such as YANG-CLI, which validates and consumes XML relevant to data modeling. myfile.xml is the sort of file YANG-CLI manages.

questions.text: Fill in the blanks to import the modules parsexml.py uses: ElementTree for the parsing, and the regular expression engine.
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 1b: import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET does the parsing, and import re is used to search for specific data.

questions.text: Fill in the blanks to parse myfile.xml and get its root element.
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 1c: ET.parse() parses the file, and getroot() returns the root element — here, <rpc>.

questions.text: What does ns hold after this line?
questions.explanation: ElementTree stores a namespaced tag as {namespace}name, so root.tag is {urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netconf:base:1.0}rpc. The regex {.*} matches the namespace in braces, braces included. Verified by running it.

questions.text: Why does the script add ns in front of each tag name in find()?
options: The elements are in the <rpc>'s XML namespace, so find("edit-config") without it finds nothing
find() needs braces around every tag name
It turns the tag name into a regular expression
It's only for readability; it doesn't change the result
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 1d. The xmlns on <rpc> applies to its children, so their real tag is {urn:...}edit-config. Running root.find("edit-config") returns None (verified).

questions.text: What does parsexml.py print?

The test-option contains: set

The default-operation contains: create

The test-option contains: merge

The test-option contains: None
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2: <default-operation>merge</default-operation> and <test-option>set</test-option>; .text reads the content between the tags. Verified by running it.

questions.text: To print the value inside an element such as <default-operation>merge</default-operation>, which attribute do you use?
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 1e: defop.text is the text content. .tag is the element's name (with namespace), and .attrib is its attributes, like {'message-id': '1'} on <rpc>.

questions.text: Which step comes first in the usual REST API workflow the lab describes?
options: Authenticate with a user/password to get a token that expires after a set time
Execute a POST to change the resource's state
Execute a GET to retrieve the resource's state
questions.explanation: Part 3 intro, in order: 1) authenticate to retrieve a token, 2) GET the resource's state as JSON, 3) modify the returned JSON, 4) POST (or PUT) to change the resource's state.

questions.text: In the token response, "expires_in":1209600 is in seconds. How long is that?
questions.explanation: 1,209,600 ÷ 86,400 seconds per day = 14 days. (refreshtokenexpires_in, 7,776,000 seconds, is 90 days.)

questions.text: Fill in the blanks to open myfile.json and parse it.
questions.code:
import json
import yaml

___ open('myfile.json','r') as json_file:
    ourjson = json.___(json_file)
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 1c: the with statement opens the file, and json.load() parses the open file. You don't need to close the file yourself; with handles opening and closing it.

questions.text: What's the difference between json.load() and json.loads()?
options: load() reads from a file object; loads() parses a string
load() parses a string; loads() reads from a file object
questions.explanation: The “s” stands for string. The script passes the open file to json.load(json_file); passing a file to json.loads() raises TypeError: the JSON object must be str, bytes or bytearray, not TextIOWrapper (verified). Part 3's intro mentions loads(), but the code uses load().
questions.warning: Upon double checking, the script uses json.load() (from a file), not loads() as Part 3's intro says.

questions.text: After ourjson = json.load(json_file), what type is ourjson?
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 1d: printing ourjson shows it is now a Python dictionary — {'access_token': '...', 'expires_in': 1209600, ...}. Step 1c says it loads into a string, but the result is a dict (checked with type()).
questions.warning: Upon double checking, json.load() gives you a dict, not a string — Step 1c's wording is off.

questions.text: How does the script read the access token out of ourjson?
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 2b: once parsed, the data is accessed with normal Python dictionary references, like ourjson['access_token'] and ourjson['expires_in'].

questions.text: What do these two lines print?

print("The access token is: {}".format(ourjson['access_token']))
print("The token expires in {} seconds.".format(ourjson['expires_in']))

questions.text: Fill in the blank to output ourjson as YAML.
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 3a: yaml.dump() serializes the Python data back out as YAML.

questions.text: What does print("\n\n---") produce?
options: Two blank lines, then ---, the start-of-document marker for YAML
A horizontal line in the terminal
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 3a: the two \n add two lines after the previous output, and --- is the three dashes that begin a YAML document.

questions.text: What does yaml.dump(ourjson) output?
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 3b: YAML writes each key as key: value on its own line, with no braces or quotes. Verified by running it. (By default yaml.dump() sorts keys alphabetically; these four already are.)

questions.text: Fill in the blank to parse myfile.yaml with PyYAML's safe loader.
questions.code:
with open('myfile.yaml','r') as yaml_file:
    ouryaml = yaml.___(yaml_file)
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 1c: yaml.safe_load() parses the file stream into a Python data structure — a dict here.

questions.text: Parsing myfile.yaml with yaml.safe_load() gives the same Python dictionary as parsing myfile.json with json.load().
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 2a prints exactly the same dictionary as Part 3 — the YAML file is the one output in Part 3. Both are just text formats for the same data. Verified by running both scripts.

questions.text: Fill in the blanks to print ouryaml as pretty-printed JSON.
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 3a: json.dumps() serializes the data to a JSON string, and the indent parameter prettifies it.

questions.text: With json.dumps(ouryaml, indent=4), how many spaces are each key indented by?
questions.explanation: indent=4 puts each key on its own line, indented 4 spaces. Without indent, json.dumps() prints everything on one line. Verified by running both.
questions.warning: Upon double checking, Part 4, Step 3b's sample shows 2-space indentation, but indent=4 really indents 4 spaces.

Parses a JSON string into Python data
Serializes Python data to a JSON string

questions.explanation: Parts 3–4: load functions parse text into Python data; dump functions serialize Python data back out. The trailing “s” in loads/dumps means string.

questions.text: What's the advantage of opening files with the with statement?
options: The file is closed automatically when the block ends
The file is opened in read-only mode automatically
The file is created if it doesn't exist
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 1c note: “There is no need to explicitly close the file as the with statement ensures proper opening and closing of the file.”
